about: Where the TF2 Voice Emulator stands. Read CLAUDE.md first, then this. The orchestrating session keeps this file; builders do not edit it.

stands.live: https://neb882.github.io/source-VOIP-converter7/ serves main (GitHub Pages from the branch root).
stands.model: The Steam profile, the voice gate and the receiver are measured (tests/REFERENCE_2026.md, findings 1-21). vaudio_celt runs the real CELT 0.11 at settings three public decoders agree on. The speex profile runs the real Speex 1.2.1 at assumed settings (quality 4, 8 kbps). vaudio_celt_high, the Speex settings and the rooms are unconfirmed.
stands.last_merged: W3-04 (2026-11-10): a file is decoded at its own sample rate, so the same file gives the same samples on every machine (docs/reports/W3-04-native-rate-decode.md). Before it, W2-01: the meter can measure a render a piece at a time.
stands.ci: The tests workflow runs on every push and can be started by hand. Until 2026-11-09 one browser check (the live recording's lag) failed by chance about once in thirty runs; W1-04 removed the cause, so a red run is a real failure. A branch made before W1-04 still has the old check until it merges main.
stands.takes: Since 2026-11-09 the owner's takes are in a private repository a session can attach (the owner knows its name; it is not named here). It holds Sets A to F as FLAC, the Set D demo, the source speech and clip, and the three test signals as played; the checksums of the Set D and F files match tests/REFERENCE_2026.md. The two songs played for Set A are there too. Not found: take1_default.flac (only the voice_maxgain 10 take of that pair; the tests accept either). The six prediction takes are not recorded yet. tests/accuracy.mjs and tests/retiming.mjs can run wherever that repository is cloned: pass its folder with --takes, and copy its signals folder into tests/testsignal/ (ignored by git).
stands.baseline: 2026-11-09, main at 61fcb92: tests/accuracy.mjs on the 16 takes of Sets B to F gives every figure of the 'Every take' table in tests/REFERENCE_2026.md to the last digit shown, so the review fixes, the demo reader and Speex moved nothing in the measured model. The Set D demo answered W1-02's open question: Steam's sequence numbers restart at 0 after each end marker (REFERENCE finding 11). Set A and tests/retiming.mjs reproduce the document too. Read block by block (2026-11-09, a scratch copy that kept each half-second block): on the owner's speech 231 of 246 blocks are within 0.5 dB and 239 agree to 0.18 dB rms; the 7 others are the quiet half-seconds where a talk spurt ends (take -48 to -52 dBFS, the game's ambience in the recording against the model's silence) or where the receiver moved a spurt. On the test signal 170 of 177 agree to 0.20 dB rms and the 7 others are the known cases of findings 13 and 14. So the accuracy table's 0.96 and 1.45 dB are those few blocks, not a general error. What is left on the modern preset for speech is when phrases start: the game started 9 of this take's spurts 100 to 340 ms early or late, which the render models only as an option (voice_retime, findings 19 and 21).
stands.priority: The owner cares most about the modern preset (the Steam profile at defaults), which they have A/B tested against the game. Work on it comes before the legacy codecs and the rooms.
stands.console: The game's 'find voice' output (2026-11-09, kept in the private repository) gives the receiver's defaults: voice_buffer_ms 100, voice_fadeouttime 0.1, voice_overdrive 2, voice_overdrivefadetime 0.4, voice_steal 2, voice_avggain 0.5, voice_maxgain 10, voice_scale 1. Its help for sv_voicecodec calls vaudio_celt '22kHz, 22kbps' and vaudio_celt_high '44kHz, 44kbps', which the celt_44 profile (256-sample frames, 120-byte packets) does not match: W3-03 checks it. The debug variables exist in this build: voice_recordtofile (writes voice_micdata.wav and voice_decompressed.wav), voice_inputfromfile (reads voice_input.wav; sv_allow_voice_from_file defaults to 1), voice_writevoices, voice_showincoming, voice_showchannels, voice_profile.
stands.phrase_timing: W3-01 (2026-11-10, from the takes alone): the receiver's queue model beats the flat 41% rule on held-out takes (speech and the Set C baseline: -9.7 against -20.0 log-likelihood over 21 transitions; the flat rule cannot chain early starts and the speech take has two chains), with L0 350 ms, a 62.5 ms silence record and a ceiling at L0. Its limits: from the source alone it reproduces 41% of speech transitions (flat rule 31%), never the whole pattern, and on 6 of 8 takes moving spurts places them worse than leaving them, because the game's pauses on speech come out about 50 ms longer than the gate model predicts. New, and in neither model: a restarted spurt plays 25 to 50 ms late and the receiver skips that much audio within half a second, on 13 of 14 restarts seen. Three constants are fitted, not understood; W3-03 reads the engine for the rule.
stands.debug_run: 2026-11-10, the owner's first run of the game's debug variables (kept in the private repository as Set G; a first reading by the orchestrator, to be checked against the engine by W3-03). With voice_showincoming and voice_showchannels the console prints every packet added to the voice channel and the channel's queued bytes on every frame. Read from it: packets are 60 ms (three frames) and a spurt's first is 160 ms; the queue never exceeds 0.5 s (22050 samples at 44.1 kHz) and 103 of 1,520 packets landed on that limit, so what did not fit was dropped (about 25 ms each); after a spurt's first packet on an empty channel the queue does not drain for 25 to 30 frames whatever arrived meanwhile (about 340 to 410 ms: the restart latency is a time, not a fill level); the mixer takes 512-sample blocks. voice_inputfromfile does nothing under the Steam codec (the owner heard only the microphone), and voice_recordtofile wrote only 5 to 8 s: no sample-exact tap of the Steam path that way. Third run (frame-rate test, 2026-11-10): the owner's fps_max is 300, and with fps_max 67, 100 and 300 the wait before a channel plays was 7, 11 and 31 ticks, against the 6 to 7, 9 to 10 and 30 the engine's rule predicts; the queue at the start was 220, 288 and 500 ms, and packets overflowed the ring only at 300 (14 of them). So the frame-rate dependence is confirmed by experiment. SourceTV did not run on the local server (no demo), so the decoder cannot be checked sample for sample from this run; its voice_decompressed.wav with the gain at 1 is the decoder's own output for one key press.
stands.receiver: W3-03 (2026-11-10, docs/reports/W3-03-engine-binary.md): the receiver's queue was read from the owner's engine file and agrees with the owner's console log (Set G) on every count checked. A voice channel is a 0.5 s ring at 44.1 kHz; overflow drops the oldest sound, heard as a skip. A packet for a speaker with no channel opens one, resets the gain to 1.0 and starts a countdown of voice_buffer_ms (100) that falls by one FRAME's duration per 15 ms TICK, so the wait before playing is about 100 ms at 67 fps, 345 ms at 233 fps and 450 ms at 300 fps, and what is queued at the start is at most 0.5 s less the 160 ms a spurt opens with: about 350 ms on a fast PC, which is the L0 the takes gave. A spurt whose first packet arrives before the ring is found empty is appended (W3-01's rule, plus a grace of one tick); otherwise the channel is freed and the next packet restarts. One sample is dropped from every packet, which is the 400 ppm every take runs fast by (not a recorder's clock). The last voice_fadeouttime (0.1 s) of a queue is faded. The gain law of findings 3 and 4 is confirmed, with small corrections: the ramp divides by 127, the block mean is an integer, a decoded block of zeros sends the gain to its cap, and the gain resets when a channel is assigned. Not found in the voice path: the [0.1, 0.8, 0.1] output stage. Legacy codecs: vaudio_celt is 22050 Hz, 512 samples, 64 bytes at complexity 5 (the app runs 10); vaudio_celt_high is 1024-sample frames in 128-byte packets fed 22050 Hz sound (the app's celt_44 runs a table row the engine never selects); the engine asks vaudio_speex for quality 3 at 11025 Hz. voice_inputfromfile is not read under the Steam codec but is under vaudio_celt (22050 Hz, 16-bit mono, beside the executable); voice_recordtofile writes up to 11.9 s per key press, after the gain.
stands.gain_exact: 2026-11-10, Set H (the owner ran vaudio_celt with a known file as the microphone, voice_maxgain 1 and then 10, voice_recordtofile on): the engine's gain rule as W3-03 read it, applied to the gain-1 recording, gives the gain-10 recording sample for sample over 291,840 samples (570 packets; only the last packet differs, and that differs between the two key presses). The integer block mean and the rule that a decoded block of zeros sends the gain to its cap are both needed for that (2,798 and 234 of the 291,840 samples differ without them; 3,309 and 745 counted over the whole file with its last packet); the divisor 127 or 128 makes no difference on this signal. The app's present rule differs on 3,032 samples. This is the first sample-exact check of any receiver stage against the game, and the gain code is shared with the Steam path. The same set shows vaudio_celt in 512-sample packets and vaudio_celt_high in 1024-sample packets, both at 22050 Hz. The app's CELT did not match it (17.7 dB); W3-08 found why.
stands.celt_exact: W3-08 (2026-11-10, docs/reports/W3-08-celt-encoder.md): the game's CELT is the source the app already pins, built with its pitch pre-filter and post-filter compiled in (the app's build has them out). With that build switch, a reset after creation, 16-bit entry points with ties to even, and the two-sample start of the engine's file reader, the project's own WebAssembly build gives Set H's vaudio_celt recording at 292,351 of 292,352 samples and its vaudio_celt_high recording at 292,789 of 292,864, the rest one step off (the orchestrator re-ran the check). vaudio_celt_high is the 44100 Hz mode with 1024-sample frames and 128-byte packets, run on 22050 Hz sound. The bundled decoder refuses any real vaudio_celt packet whose filter flag is set, so a demo's CELT voice does not decode today where the voice is pitched. All of this is built by W3-06 as amended, after W2-02 merges.
stands.mixer_output: W3-07 (2026-11-10, docs/reports/W3-07-mixer-output.md), read from the owner's engine.dll and checked against Sets B and D: the mixer runs at a fixed 44100 Hz in 512-sample blocks; a voice channel is copied in sample for sample (no rate conversion, no interpolation, no spatialisation, no filter) at 255/256 truncated toward zero; the sum of voice and game sound is clipped at +-32767, then multiplied by volume and rounded. voice_overdrive never touches the voice itself. The roll-off above 12 kHz that the model fits with the 3-tap [0.1, 0.8, 0.1] is not in the game: it is the system mixer's linear interpolation from 44100 to the device's 48000 Hz (flat tops stay exactly on the ceiling; a 1 kHz tone has images at 2900 and 4900 Hz at -64 to -67 dB in five recordings, predicted -65.4 and -66.2; response sinc squared, equal to the 3-tap within 0.1 dB up to 13 kHz and 1.1 dB lower at 18 kHz). On a 44100 Hz device there would be no roll-off (inferred, no take). Listener B is explained: volume 0.11 (ceiling 3604 = round(32767 x 0.11)) and voice_scale 0.77 on that PC, which with the engine's gain rule gives its staircase; REFERENCE's 'about 0.077' and finding 15's reading of B are wrong. Not modelled and not needed for the takes: the room and water DSP a voice also passes through.
stands.steam_sender: W3-09 (2026-11-10, docs/reports/W3-09-steam-voice.md), read from the owner's steamclient64.dll and checked against Set G's logs and Set D's demo. Capture at 24000 Hz in steps of 750 samples; each Steam frame (about 55.85 ms) takes the whole steps captured since the last as one chunk; the gate is open when the chunk's mean of |x| is at least 1.0% of full scale or its peak at least 15%; an opening sends the last 100 ms (2400 samples) before the chunk with it; the hold is 0.4 s of wall-clock time; key up is followed by 0.5 s more capture; one chunk is one message; frames of 480 are cut from kept plus chunk; the end marker resets the encoder and the sequence number. Encoder: libopus 1.1.4, VOIP, 32 kbit/s, DTX on, complexity default 9 (the project's build gives the same packets at 8 to 10), 16-bit entry points. Decoder: concealment capped at 10 frames; the 24 to 44.1 kHz step is libswresample at its defaults, called once per packet with a flush, which gives the logs' sample counts exactly (7056, 2646, 882). Not yet tested by the owner: Steam's console variables mic_inputfile (a file in place of the microphone under the Steam codec) and @voice_spew_activity_check; clips for that run are in the private repository.
stands.speex_module: W3-09 section 5, read from a vaudio_speex module the owner supplied (32-bit, from HL2DM): Speex 1.0.2 (float), narrowband, the engine's quality 3 mapped to Speex quality 4, 160-sample frames in 20 bytes, constant bit rate, no VAD or DTX, enhancement on, complexity default. The module does not resample: 11025 Hz sound goes into the 8 kHz codec as it is, so a frame is 14.51 ms, the real rate 11.025 kbit/s and the band reaches 5.5 kHz; decoded floats are truncated to 16 bits with no clamp. The app's speex profile (1.2.1 with resampling to 8000 Hz) is to be rebuilt accordingly (W3-12). No recording of Speex can be made from a current game: asked for vaudio_speex, the engine starts vaudio_celt (Set I, a third recording the corrected CELT build reproduces, 145,919 of 145,920 samples; the fall-back was then found in TF2's engine.dll, W3-09 section 6).

in_flight.note: Built; the private acceptance passes on each head (Set H through tests/gain-exact.mjs: 0 of 291,840 samples differ); the accuracy table on all takes reads as before. A second read of the gain function (2026-11-10) settled what the recording cannot see, all READ: every float operation is single precision, one at a time, in the app's order; the per-sample product is a 32-bit multiply that wraps (the app now wraps too; it matters only when maxgain x scale squared passes about 512); the reset writes unity for the first block whatever voice_scale is and the three settings are read only at a reset. Review: an implementation written from the order agreed on 10,000 seeded cases and reproduced all 47 golden hashes; a 30-minute render is as fast as before. The builder is closing the last two low points (the live chain's window of sent flags, four test gaps). Then pull request.

The Node suites load audio.js and constants.js in a vm context, which makes Math-heavy code about 12 times slower than the page runs it (found by W2-01's builder). Loading them another way could cut pnpm test's minute, if the results stay bit for bit the same.

tests/accuracy.mjs could report its level figure without the half-second blocks that hold a talk spurt's end or a moved spurt, next to the figure it gives now: on speech that is 0.18 dB against 0.96, and the second number reads as a model error it is not.

deferred.finding: video.js writes every kept track with sample description 1 (the review's finding 15).
deferred.why: Only files with more than one sample description are affected, and none is at hand to prove it.

deferred.finding: tests/verify.js section 10b checks the live chain's loss model against the render's frame for frame, but the live chain draws the mask only for frames the gate sends, so with the gate on the two lose different frames for the same seed (found by the W1-03 planner).
deferred.why: Neither is wrong, and the rates agree; the check just does not cover the chain as it runs. Fix the wording or the check when the live chain is next touched.

deferred.finding: demo.js: after a pause with no end marker in which the sequence numbers continue, one duplicated or out-of-order packet counts as a sequence break that arrives late, so the run is split and the rest placed at its tick (W1-02's review, finding 6).
deferred.why: It needs both an unmarked pause with continuing numbers and a duplicate or reordered voice packet, which Source's network channel is believed to drop before SourceTV records them. Not verified on a real demo. A fix would be to ignore a number that falls just behind the expected one.

deferred.finding: The browser suite's live-recording check allows a lag of one sample; W1-04's data (58 recordings, peak at 0 every time, fractional 0.00-0.04) would support exactly zero. An earlier note here blamed a half-sample spread on the live chain and the render starting at different points: that spread came from Chromium's beep, not from the chain.
deferred.why: The order asked for one sample, and tests/verify.js pins the delay to the sample in Node. Tighten it when the live chain is next touched, after a few CI runs on GitHub's Chromium confirm the zero.

deferred.finding: filerate.js does not read WebM or Matroska (video.js does not parse them), so those files are still decoded at the audio device's rate, with a console line. A plain AAC file in ADTS at 24 kHz or less is decoded at twice its rate (the rule that keeps an HE-AAC file's upper band); HE-AAC itself was reasoned, not measured, and Firefox and Safari were not checked.
deferred.why: Each only resamples, as every file was before; none gives a wrong pitch or length.

retired_rules.why: From the first version, for memory. An audio or video file whose sound is longer than 10 minutes is refused, even though a video may be 1 GB, and a demo keeps only a speaker's first 10 minutes. W1-03 planned what replaces it: the W2 orders.

retired_rules.rule: A profile models only what current TF2 can confirm, so Speex stays a stand-in.
retired_rules.why: It contradicted 'every profile runs a real codec'. A real codec at documented, unconfirmed settings is how vaudio_celt_high already ships. W1-01.

retired_rules.rule: demo.js must match the Rust tool byte for byte.
retired_rules.why: The Rust tool was written first; demo.js is what users run and CI tests. The rule was used as a reason to leave a defect alone. W1-02.

rules_challenged_and_kept: No leaked engine source: it would answer the legacy codecs' settings and the receiver's queue rules quickly, but the repository is public under the owner's name and its claims rest on recordings and public packets.
Pinned codecs, seeded renders, registered predictions, the source timeline by default, no uploads, a failing test with every fix.

decisions.what: The first target for long sources is 30 minutes at 48 kHz for audio and video files (a sample budget, so 15 minutes at 96 kHz), the whole voice of a demo up to 60 minutes, and 30 minutes for a recording. Where the browser reports under 8 GB of device memory, the budget stays at 10 minutes.
decisions.why: After the render and the meter stream, loading the file is the peak (about 4.5 float copies of it), which a desktop tab can hold for 30 minutes and a phone cannot. The owner can overrule any of these numbers; they are constants in app/core.js (W2-03).

decisions.what: Sources up to 10 minutes keep process() until the stream has proved itself; then one path.
decisions.why: The registered predictions and every test depend on today's renders. W2-02 records golden hashes so the switch can be shown to change nothing.

decisions.what: Work is split by model (docs/PIPELINE.md, 'Which model does what'): builders and reviewers on the builders' model, where a written check says whether the work is right; plans, the skeptic, the reading of evidence and the last read of each diff on the stronger model the orchestrating session runs on. The orchestrator works at high effort.
decisions.why: The owner asked that the stronger model be used to the full. Its vendor's published comparison puts the two models a few points apart on agentic coding and far apart on long unattended work, scientific computing and research, at twice the price per token. W1-03's plan was written on the builders' model and reviewed on the stronger one; from now on it is the other way round.

decisions.what: The owner expects to switch the orchestrating session back to the builders' model for cost. The pipeline is written so the split survives the switch: the stronger model's roles become agents started on it.
decisions.why: The owner said so. Before the switch, the session uses the stronger model on what only it should settle: reading the baseline against the takes and writing the model questions as orders.

decisions.what: The owner's standard is an exact recreation by any means. The orchestrator will not use leaked engine source; the owner supplied their own install's engine and codec files and the game's 'find voice' output, and reading those is allowed (CLAUDE.md, hard rules).
decisions.why: The receiver's queue and the legacy codecs' settings are in those files, and the public SDK has neither.

decisions.what: The owner left the choice of further improvements to the orchestrator. In order: (1) a sample-exact check of the codec stage with the game's own debug commands, once W3-03 says what they read and write; (2) phrase timing (W3-01, W3-03), and re-timing on by default for the modern preset if the engine's rule is found; (3) sources decoded at the file's own rate (W3-04, started); (4) the unverified parts (rooms, vaudio_celt_high, the Speex settings) verified from the game files or moved under a label; (5) the second PC's peaks 2.5 dB above the model's clamp (Listener B) explained; (6) a look at the page for a simpler first screen.
decisions.why: Exactness on the modern preset is the owner's standard; each item either proves it more strictly or removes a place where the page claims more than is shown.

decisions.what: From the receiver plan (docs/reports/W3-02-plan.md): on the page the modern preset will render the game's timeline by default (fps_max 300, voice_buffer_ms 100) with the source's timeline one setting away; a video source and the engine's own default (process() with no option) keep the source's timeline; the flat 41% rule is retired when that lands. The queue test's fixture built from the owner's logs stays in the private repository; the public suite runs a synthetic log and the orchestrator runs the private replay.
decisions.why: The owner's standard is what the game does, and the queue is now the engine's rule, confirmed on every tick of the logs and by the frame-rate test. Sound leading the picture by up to 0.35 s would be worse than the timing it fixes. The fixture shows when the owner was speaking; nothing is lost by keeping it private.
